newsitem.title: UK: Copper tries a new rally, awaits Sumitomo ambush.
newsitem.headline: Copper tries a new rally, awaits Sumitomo ambush.

text.p: Speculators who bet that demand for industrial metals is strong enough to lift the price of the flagship copper futures contract began another bid to buy it higher on Monday.

In an unfolding piece of theatre in the London Metal Exchange (LME) it was uncertain whether they would be ambushed by selling from banks that have been assigned to unwind a long position built up by Japan's Yasuo Hamanaka.
The star trader at metals group Sumitomo Corp had hoarded copper before, in June, American regulators suggested to his Japanese employees that his high price trading strategy was irregular.
Sumitomo then fired him as an alleged rogue trader who had lost it $2.6 billion and asked several banks to dispose of his hoard.
Copper prices renewed a rally on the LME on Monday, buoyed by expectations of news of another drop in world warehouse stocks on Tuesday, traders and analysts said.
But all base metal markets finished the day below the highs as softening nearby spreads on copper undermined the complex.
"Copper looked set to have a look at $2,000 (a tonne) but the easing spread was the main inhibitive factor," said Robin Bhar, analyst at LME ring dealers Brandeis.
"The nearby rates haven't really moved up, so there does not appear to be too much panic in the market despite stocks being at very low levels," he added.
The worry is that, as happened last week, any rally above $2000 will hit Sumitomo-linked selling and copper will take another tumble, like one of $100 a tonne last Tuesday.
Gold closed in London at $379.05 an ounce after $377.65 on Friday. It consolidated in tight range after ticking higher overnight and early on Monday following last week's dive.
Investment funds took the view that the benchmark Brent Blend of crude oil, after a recent decline, was unlikely to return quickly to a $25.06 post-Gulf War peak of two weeks ago.
But nobody was willing to sell the oil market too hard when heating fuel stocks are low and cold weather could hit the north east of the United States at any day.
So Brent was holding at around $22.50 on Monday.
Other world commodity markets had a dull day with coffee and cocoa just easier but sugar steadying from a technical slide.
